title: Pattern: Real-Time Updates
summary: Keep clients up to date with polling, SSE or WebSockets. Route events to the right server with pub/sub and help reconnecting clients catch up.
body:
A chat message, a live score or a moving driver's marker should not wait for a page refresh. These features often need updates within about a second. Since ordinary HTTP requests start with the client, your design needs two answers: how the server reaches the client, and how an event finds the server holding that client's connection. Interviewers will ask about both.

## Client delivery options

| Option | How it works | Latency | Good for | Trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Short polling | Client asks every N seconds | Up to N s | Low-frequency updates, simplest | Wasted requests; load scales with users × frequency |
| Long polling | Server holds the request until data arrives or ~30 s timeout | Near real time | Infrequent events, restrictive networks | One request per message; reconnect overhead |
| Server-Sent Events (SSE) | One long-lived HTTP response streaming events server → client | Near real time | Feeds, scores, notifications, LLM token streams | One-way; text only; client sends via normal HTTP |
| WebSocket | Upgraded TCP connection, full duplex | Lowest | Chat, games, collaborative editing | Stateful connections; load balancer and deploy complexity |
| WebRTC | Peer-to-peer media/data after signaling via your server | Lowest, P2P | Voice/video calls | Needs STUN/TURN for NAT traversal; complex; not for server fan-out |

Start with the simplest option that meets the latency goal. SSE uses plain HTTP, reconnects automatically in the browser and sends `Last-Event-ID` so the server can resume from retained events. Choose WebSockets when clients also send frequent messages over the same channel.

## Server-side fan-out

One server can find a connection with a local lookup. With 100 gateways holding 50k connections each, the sender and recipient usually land on different machines. Separate **connection gateways** (sockets, little logic) from **application services** (validation, persistence and recipient selection), then connect them with pub/sub.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Sender"] --> G1["Gateway 1"]
    G1 --> S["Message service"]
    S --> DB[("Message store")]
    S --> PS[["Pub/sub: Redis or Kafka"]]
    PS --> G2["Gateway 2"]
    PS --> G3["Gateway 3"]
    G2 --> B["Recipient B"]
    G3 --> C["Recipient C"]
    REG[("Connection registry")] -.-> S
```

The sender's gateway forwards to the message service, which persists the message with a per-conversation sequence number before publishing. Subscribed gateways push it to recipients B and C. A connection registry can identify each user's gateway, letting the service target that gateway's channel instead of broadcasting everywhere.

### Routing choices

- **Channel per user or room, gateways subscribe on demand.** On connect, the gateway subscribes to `user:{id}` or `room:{id}`. Publishers need not track locations. Redis pub/sub supports many channels but is fire-and-forget: disconnected subscribers miss messages.
- **Connection registry.** Store `user_id → gateway_id` in Redis, refresh its TTL by heartbeat and publish to `gateway:{id}`. Routing is explicit, but every connect and disconnect must update the registry.
- **Consistent hashing.** Hash each user or room onto a gateway ring so services compute the owner without a lookup. Adding or removing a gateway moves about 1/N of users, who must reconnect. This needs a routing layer, such as a balancer hashing a user token, and works best with infrequent membership changes.
- **Kafka** suits durable, replayable streams: partition by conversation and let gateways or a delivery service consume. Budget for higher latency and per-partition consumer limits.

### Fan-out on write vs on read

**Fan-out on write** pushes an update to each follower's inbox or socket when it is sent: fast reads, expensive writes for accounts with millions of followers. **Fan-out on read** fetches from followed sources when a viewer reads: cheaper writes, slower reads. A hybrid pushes normal accounts and pulls celebrity updates.

## Presence, reconnects and catch-up

Phones switch networks, laptops sleep and gateways redeploy. Reconnection is part of the normal flow, not an edge case.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant G as Gateway
    participant S as Message service
    C->>G: Connect, last_seq 41
    G->>S: Fetch conversation after 41
    S-->>G: Messages 42 to 45
    G-->>C: Replay 42 to 45
    G->>S: Subscribe live channel
    S-->>G: Message 46
    G-->>C: Push 46, client acks
```

The client reports its highest **contiguous sequence number**: the last message before any gap in what it has received. The gateway replays what follows from durable storage. The diagram separates replay and live delivery for readability; doing them strictly in that order could miss an event between the fetch and subscription. Subscribe and buffer live events first. Replay through a **durable high-water mark**, a known persisted sequence boundary, then merge the buffered events by sequence. Skip duplicates and fetch any remaining gaps from storage. Bound the buffer and restart catch-up if it overflows. Durable storage owns the truth; pub/sub provides the fast path.

- **Presence:** heartbeat about every 30 s; refresh `presence:{user}` with a roughly 60 s TTL. Expiry marks the user offline. Publish changes only to people viewing that contact, since presence fan-out can exceed message traffic.
- **Reconnect storms:** a failed gateway can send 50k clients back at once. Use exponential backoff with jitter. On planned deploys, stop accepting connections and spread client reconnects over a few minutes.
- **Offline users:** persist first, send a push notification as a nudge and sync when the client opens.

## Failure modes and interview mistakes

- Treating Redis pub/sub as durable. Disconnected subscribers miss messages; retain them and support catch-up.
- Reaching for WebSockets when one-way SSE or long polling would be simpler.
- Forgetting connection-aware balancing (such as least connections), long idle timeouts and graceful draining for WebSockets.
- Broadcasting to every gateway: cost grows as messages × gateways. Route by registry, channel or hash.
- Ordering by client timestamps rather than a per-conversation sequence from the single writer.
- Skipping fleet sizing: 10M connections at about 50k per gateway need roughly 200 gateways before headroom.

## How to use it in an interview

1. Pick the protocol from traffic direction, latency target and update frequency.
2. Estimate gateways: concurrent users ÷ connections per gateway. Tens of thousands per gateway is a starting assumption; check memory per connection.
3. Draw gateways, the message service, durable storage and pub/sub. Trace an event to the right gateway.
4. Explain sequence-based catch-up, TTL heartbeats for presence and fan-out for large audiences.

Be ready for: "What happens when a gateway crashes?", "How do you guarantee ordering?" and "How does a user on three devices get the message?" Subscribe every device connection to the user channel and track a read cursor per device.

## Interview exercise

Design live score updates for a sports app: 5M concurrent viewers during a final, one score event every few seconds, plus a chat room per match with 200k active chatters. Choose a protocol for each feature, size the gateway fleet, and explain how a viewer who loses signal for 20 seconds catches up.

keyTakeaways: Pick the simplest client protocol that meets the latency and direction requirements; SSE covers many one-way cases.
Separate connection gateways from application logic and route events between them with pub/sub, a registry or consistent hashing.
Persist before publishing: pub/sub is the fast path, the durable store is the source of truth.
Reconnect from the last contiguous sequence, overlap replay with live subscription, and deduplicate by sequence so the handoff cannot lose a message.
Use TTL heartbeats for presence and jittered backoff to survive reconnect storms.
